nodes.name: Deltoid
nodes.location: Caps the shoulder at the front, outer side and back, from the collarbone and the shoulder blade down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Its front part raises your arm forward and turns it inward, its outer part raises the arm out to the side, and its back part moves the arm backward and turns it outward. It also helps hold the shoulder steady.
nodes.shapeNote: Together its three parts make up most of the rounded outline of the shoulder. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for its three parts.
The three parts are a teaching simplification: anatomy studies divide the deltoid into more segments, five to eight in one study of its nerve branches, and the count differs between people.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Superficial over the whole shoulder; references call it easily observed and palpated and say it gives the shoulder its rounded contour (kenhub.deltoid, elsevier.deltoid, statpearls.deltoid).
nodes.layerCheck: Parent node, not drawn (layer '—' in §1.2). All three parts are surface muscles, so 'surface' is the honest value if the type needs one.

nodes.name: Anterior deltoid
nodes.location: Front of the shoulder, from the outer third of the collarbone down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Raises your arm forward and turns it inward. It also helps bring a raised arm across the front of the chest and helps raise the arm out to the side.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the front of the rounded shoulder outline, beside the upper chest, where a groove separates it from the pectoralis major. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Presses and front raises load it together with the upper chest; how the work splits between them changes with the exercise and the bench angle.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Just under the skin at the front of the shoulder and bounded from the chest by the deltopectoral groove (kenhub.deltoid, radiopaedia.deltopectoral_groove).

nodes.name: Lateral deltoid
nodes.location: Outer side of the shoulder, from the outer edge of the bony tip of the shoulder (the acromion) down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Raises your arm out to the side, doing most of the lifting in that movement, with the supraspinatus working alongside it.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the outer curve of the shoulder. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Studies call this part the middle, lateral or medial deltoid; all three names mean the same part.
Raising the arm out to the side also works the supraspinatus, which lies under the trapezius and the bony tip of the shoulder.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Just under the skin on the outer side of the shoulder (kenhub.deltoid, elsevier.deltoid_acromial).

nodes.name: Posterior deltoid
nodes.location: Back of the shoulder, from the bony ridge of the shoulder blade (its spine) down to the outer side of the upper arm.
nodes.whatItDoes: Moves a raised arm backward, brings the arm back and down from in front of the body, and turns the arm outward.
nodes.shapeNote: May contribute to the back of the rounded shoulder outline, over parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: In one comparison it worked harder in a reverse fly than in a seated row or a pulldown.
Turning the arm outward loads it together with the infraspinatus and teres minor.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Just under the skin at the back of the shoulder; it covers parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor rather than being covered (kenhub.deltoid, kenhub.infraspinatus, kenhub.teres_minor).

nodes.name: Rotator cuff
nodes.location: Four muscles from the shoulder blade to the upper end of the upper-arm bone, wrapping the shoulder joint at the front, the top and the back.
nodes.whatItDoes: Holds the ball of the upper-arm bone in its shallow socket while the arm moves, and turns the arm inward and outward.
nodes.shapeNote: Mostly deep, under the deltoid and the trapezius, so as a group it has little or no contour of its own; only parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor reach the surface, on the back of the shoulder blade. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: A group, not a muscle: work is counted for the four muscles inside it.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Supraspinatus and subscapularis are covered; parts of the infraspinatus and teres minor are not covered by other muscles (kenhub.infraspinatus, kenhub.teres_minor).
nodes.layerCheck: Parent node, not drawn (layer '—' in §1.2). All four members are 'deep' in §1.2, so 'deep' is the honest value if the type needs one.

nodes.name: Supraspinatus
nodes.location: Top of the shoulder blade, above its bony ridge and under the trapezius; its tendon runs under the bony tip of the shoulder to the top of the upper-arm bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Helps raise your arm out to the side, working with the deltoid. It also helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies under the trapezius and the bony tip of the shoulder, so it has little or no visible contour of its own.
caveats: Raising the arm to the side works it together with the deltoid; testing studies found positions that raise its share relative to the deltoid, and none of them was an exercise.
Anatomy texts teach that it starts the movement, but in one muscle-activity study it switched on together with the deltoid, not before it. The deltoid does most of the lifting.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Covered by the trapezius, with its tendon under the acromion (kenhub.supraspinatus, statpearls.supraspinatus).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep: supported (under the trapezius; kenhub.supraspinatus). No outcrop claimed, none found.

nodes.name: Infraspinatus
nodes.location: Back of the shoulder blade, below its bony ridge; its tendon crosses the back of the shoulder joint to the upper end of the upper-arm bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your arm outward, and helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: Covers most of the back of the shoulder blade below its ridge. Parts of it lie under the trapezius, the back of the deltoid and the latissimus dorsi, so it has little separately visible contour of its own; where it is not covered it may contribute to the contour on the back of the shoulder blade. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: Turning the arm outward works it together with the teres minor and the back of the deltoid; how the work splits between them changes with arm position and is not known exactly.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Kenhub places it deep to the trapezius and only parts of the deltoid and latissimus dorsi, which leaves part of it uncovered on the back of the shoulder blade (kenhub.infraspinatus).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep with a back-view surface outcrop: supported by kenhub.infraspinatus ('deep to trapezius, and parts of the deltoid and latissimus dorsi'). elsevier.infraspinatus says deep to the trapezius and deltoid without saying 'parts of'; not a contradiction of the outcrop, but less specific.

nodes.name: Teres minor
nodes.location: Outer edge of the shoulder blade on the back, just below the infraspinatus and above the teres major; its tendon reaches the upper end of the upper-arm bone from behind.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your arm outward, alongside the infraspinatus, and helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket.
nodes.shapeNote: Narrow, and partly covered by the back of the deltoid, so it has little separately visible contour of its own; it lies between the infraspinatus above and the teres major below. Visible shape also depends on neighbouring muscles, body fat and individual anatomy.
caveats: It turns the arm outward together with the infraspinatus, so outward-turning work loads both.
Not the teres major, the muscle just below it, which belongs to the back.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: Kenhub says the deltoid covers its upper outer part, leaving the rest near the surface; it is narrow and lies between the infraspinatus and teres major (kenhub.teres_minor, statpearls.teres_minor).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep with a back-view surface outcrop: supported by kenhub.teres_minor (the deltoid covers its superolateral aspect). statpearls.teres_minor calls it 'located deep to the deltoid' without qualification; the two read differently, and the outcrop rests on Kenhub. §7.2 already allows it to be list-only if it cannot hold a 44 px square.

nodes.name: Subscapularis
nodes.location: Front, rib-facing surface of the shoulder blade; its tendon crosses the front of the shoulder joint to the upper-arm bone.
nodes.whatItDoes: Turns your arm inward, and helps hold the ball of the upper-arm bone in its socket. It is the largest muscle of the rotator cuff.
nodes.shapeNote: Lies on the rib-facing side of the shoulder blade, under other structures, so it has little or no visible contour of its own.
caveats: Its upper and lower parts can be recorded separately; in one exercise study arm position changed which part worked harder, while studies of clinical tests disagree on whether the two parts differ.
nodes.surfaceVisibilityReason: On the costal surface of the scapula, behind the serratus anterior and the shoulder joint (elsevier.subscapularis, kenhub.subscapularis).
nodes.layerCheck: Deep: supported. Drawing note (not a §1.2 change): from the front only its tendon and outer part cross in front of the joint (statpearls.subscapularis); the belly lies behind the rib cage in a front view.

actions.plainDescription: Raises the arm out to the side.

actions.label: Shoulder extension
actions.plainDescription: Brings the arm down and back from in front of the body, and on behind it.

actions.label: Horizontal adduction
actions.plainDescription: Moves an arm held out at shoulder height forward and across the chest.

actions.label: Horizontal abduction
actions.plainDescription: Moves an arm held out in front at shoulder height back and out to the side.

actions.label: Shoulder external rotation
actions.plainDescription: Turns the upper arm outward on its long axis: with the elbow bent, the hand swings away from the belly.

actions.label: Shoulder internal rotation
actions.plainDescription: Turns the upper arm inward on its long axis: with the elbow bent, the hand swings toward the belly.

actions.label: Scapular upward rotation
actions.plainDescription: Turns the shoulder blade so the shoulder socket faces up, as the arm rises overhead.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Deltoid Muscle (Elzanie and Varacallo)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (introduction and part of the function section): a large triangular muscle that forms the shoulder's rounded contour and is a key player in shoulder stability and motion; its three parts together help raise the arm past about 15 degrees, but the deltoid cannot start abduction because its fibres run parallel to the humerus; the anterior and posterior parts stabilise the arm during abduction while the lateral part does most of the lifting from about 15 to 100 degrees. Listed as updated 30 Jan 2024. The fibre-by-fibre flexion, rotation and extension actions were not seen in this article's visible text; the point-of-care copy (statpearls.com/point-of-care/20331) is behind a login.

sources.title: Hik and Ackland, The moment arms of the muscles spanning the glenohumeral joint: a systematic review (Journal of Anatomy 234(1):1-15)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract): pooled moment arms of the deltoid, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major and the four rotator cuff muscles during abduction, flexion and axial rotation; the anterior and middle deltoid sub-regions had the largest humeral elevator moment arms of all muscles during coronal- and scapular-plane abduction and during flexion; the posterior deltoid and teres minor can act as abductors or adductors depending on arm position; infraspinatus and teres minor oppose subscapularis in a transverse-plane force couple that compresses the humeral head into the glenoid. sources.title: Deltoid segments defined by axillary nerve branching (Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, British volume, supplement abstract; authors not confirmed)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (conference abstract): 44 deltoids from 22 embalmed adult cadavers divided by the axillary nerve branch supplying each portion: eight major divisions in 3, seven in 22 of 44, six in 14 and five in 5; the authors conclude that a segmentation into five to eight major segments is found, and cite mechanomyographic work describing at least seven functional segments in a muscle usually taught as three. Exact title, year and authors not shown: the second review saw the abstract's counts again but no author names, and a search under Audenaert and Barbaix did not find it. Audenaert and Barbaix wrote a 2008 commentary, 'Separate segments within the deltoid muscle: anatomical variants or wishful thinking?' (International Journal of Shoulder Surgery, PMC2840820), which says dissection of the bundles is largely a matter of interpretation; whether they also wrote this abstract is unconfirmed, so the title no longer names them.

sources.title: Coratella et al., An Electromyographic Analysis of Lateral Raise Variations and Frontal Raise in Competitive Bodybuilders (International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(17):6015, 2020)
sources.notes: Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract, two searches): ten competitive bodybuilders; surface EMG of the anterior, medial (lateral) and posterior deltoid, pectoralis major, upper trapezius and triceps brachii during lateral raises with the humerus externally rotated, neutral and internally rotated, a lateral raise with the elbow flexed, and a frontal raise. Concentric phase: anterior deltoid greater in the frontal raise than in all others; medial deltoid greater in the neutral lateral raise than in the externally rotated, frontal and flexed-elbow versions; posterior deltoid greater in the internally rotated lateral raise than in all others; similar patterns in the eccentric phase. The abstract's conclusion also says humeral external rotation increases anterior and medial deltoid activation, which reads against the medial result unless it compares with internal rotation; the claims rely only on the results lines. The PubMed id is read from an index record (OLB-PM-32824894), not from PubMed itself; the DOI was not shown. Acute activity, not growth.

sources.title: Campos, Vianna, Guimaraes, Oliveira, Hernandez-Mosqueira, da Silva and Marchetti, Different Shoulder Exercises Affect the Activation of Deltoid Portions in Resistance-Trained Individuals (Journal of Human Kinetics 75:5-14, 2020)

sources.title: Chalmers et al., The champagne toast position isolates the supraspinatus better than the Jobe test (Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery 25(2):322-329, 2016)

sources.title: Reed, Cathers, Halaki and Ginn, Does supraspinatus initiate shoulder abduction? (Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology 23(2):425-429, 2013)
sources.notes: Added by the second review. Checked via web-search results on 19 Oct 2026 (abstract, as listed by the Australian Catholic University repository): EMG of seven shoulder muscles in 14 volunteers during abduction in three planes at 25, 50 and 75 percent of maximum load; all muscles were activated before movement onset; supraspinatus, infraspinatus, upper and lower trapezius, serratus anterior and deltoid had similar initial activation times and subscapularis was later; the authors conclude that the supraspinatus is recruited before abduction but not earlier than the deltoid, and that the statement that it initiates abduction is misleading. A 2018 biomechanics review agrees. One other study, not identified by the search, reported the supraspinatus switching on before the middle deltoid in dumbbell movements. PubMed id and DOI not shown. Muscle-activity timing, not how much each muscle lifts.

deviations.subject: §1.2 shoulders region actions
deviations.finding: The evidence names holding the head of the upper-arm bone in its socket as the rotator cuff's core function, and §1.2 lists no action for it, so the cuff's node actions can show only rotation and abduction. The forearm modelled the same kind of role as an action (forearm.distal_radioulnar_stabilization, PQ, assist).

kenhub.rotator_cuff ('main function ... stabilize and center the humeral head')
deviations.proposal: If the adversarial review accepts it: add 'shoulder.humeral_head_stabilization' (joint 'Shoulder', label 'Steadies the ball of the shoulder in its socket', plain description 'Helps keep the ball of the upper-arm bone pressed into its shallow socket while the arm moves.') to the shoulders' region actions, with assist rows for the four cuff muscles resting on their function claims. Not applied in this dossier: §1.2 is unchanged and no node action uses it.
deviations.secondReview: The second review agrees that the sources name holding the humeral head in its socket as the cuff's core function and that the forearm modelled such a role as an assist action. Adding it is a model decision, not an evidence one: steadying credit is counted apart from direct work in every version's methodNotes, so the mappings lane would need rules for when a press or row earns it. Left to the adversarial review.

jek.reed2013_supraspinatus_onset, ajsm.pennock2011_subscapularis_tests: PubMed id and DOI not shown; txstate.deltoid: only the posterior-portion line seen (second review).
disagreements: Starting abduction. StatPearls (deltoid) says the deltoid cannot start abduction and Elsevier (acromial part) says the supraspinatus is needed to start it; Kenhub says the supraspinatus is essential for the early range. The second review found an EMG study of 14 people (Reed et al. 2013) in which the supraspinatus switched on together with the deltoid and other shoulder muscles, not before them; its authors call the textbook statement misleading, while one other study (not identified) reported the supraspinatus first. Wording: the lateral deltoid and supraspinatus function claims and the supraspinatus caveat state the textbook teaching, attributed, beside that EMG finding; the node copy no longer says the supraspinatus starts the movement.

Teres minor cover. StatPearls: 'located deep to the deltoid'; Kenhub: the deltoid covers its superolateral aspect. The appearance claim says the deltoid covers its upper outer part (Kenhub) and the outcrop in §1.2 rests on Kenhub.

Infraspinatus as a rotator. A 2024 case report's introduction (PMC11013571, 'Novel Muscle in Infraspinous Fossa') says it makes only a minor contribution to lateral rotation and mainly stabilises; StatPearls, Elsevier and Kenhub list external rotation as its action. Not cited; the claim keeps the reference texts' action and also states the stabilising role.

Coratella 2020. The results lines say the medial deltoid was more active in the neutral lateral raise than the externally rotated one; the conclusion line says external rotation increases anterior and medial deltoid activation (probably against internal rotation). The lateral-deltoid selectivity claim uses only the results lines.

Rodriguez-Ridao 2020. The abstract's overall conclusion says the flat bench gives similar pectoralis and anterior deltoid activity, while the conclusion quoted from the full text says inclines above 45 degrees raise anterior deltoid activity. The claim states the incline finding and the authors' conclusion only.

Anterior deltoid at low abduction angles. Physiopedia says the clavicular and spinal parts adduct below about 60 degrees and abduct above it; the moment-arm studies rank the anterior part among the most effective abductors. The anterior deltoid's abduction row is 'assist', and no abduction row is given to the posterior part.

Subscapularis tests. Tokish 2003 found the belly-press and lift-off tests favoured different parts; Pennock 2011 (20 people) found no difference between the two parts in three tests. The second review cites both and the claim says they disagree.

A generated summary (Q25) said the posterior deltoid's external rotation was found only on a flashcard site, while Elsevier, Loyola and Kenhub each list it. The specific references are cited; this is an example of the summaries' limits.

Supraspinatus testing positions. Both studies' titles say a position 'isolates' the supraspinatus, but what they measured is its activity relative to the deltoid's, and Chalmers 2016 found its own activity highest at 90 degrees. The claim and caveat say 'share relative to the deltoid', not 'isolate'.

Moment-arm summaries. Generated summaries of the Hik and Ackland review gave the teres minor as an internal rotator, and the posterior deltoid and supraspinatus as internal rotators in neutral; Ackland and Pandy 2011 and Kuechle et al. (PubMed 10758292) found the infraspinatus and teres minor the main external rotators and the subscapularis the main internal rotator. The review is cited only for its force-couple line; 'only internal rotator of the cuff' is attributed to anatomy references.
Soylu 2025. The paper reports 32 participants; its trial registry entry lists 15. The claim uses the paper's count.
deliberatelyNotClaimed: Horizontal abduction for the infraspinatus and teres minor: Elsevier lists it ('transversely abducts') and nothing else seen does; left out of node actions, as the forearm left out minor actions.
Weak external rotation by the supraspinatus (StatPearls 'possible weak contribution'): left out.
Adduction by the teres minor and subscapularis: said in their function claims, but shoulder.adduction is not a shoulders region action (it belongs to the chest and back).
Horizontal abduction by the lateral deltoid (Physiopedia; Botton found more middle-deltoid activity in the reverse peck deck than the pulldown): not claimed.
Variation claims for the rotator cuff: infraspinatus and teres minor fusion and accessory subscapularis slips were found only as single-specimen case reports (Wikipedia read, not cited).
A teres minor selectivity claim: no study recording it on its own was seen with results (Reinold 2004's results were not shown; a physiotherapy blog's account was not used).
Trebs 2010 (incline bench): seen only secondhand; not cited.
IMAIOS deltoid: its lines were merged with other sites in the summary, so they were not attributed or cited.
No clinical content: tear rates and testing accuracy are not stated as claims; the testing studies are cited only for what they measured in healthy people.

Second review: the sentence 'Bench angle therefore belongs in how a press is described' was taken out of shoulders.anterior_deltoid.selectivity.2; it is a recommendation for the variants lane (record bench angle on presses), not a finding.

Second review: horizontal abduction for the infraspinatus now has a second source in principle (Kuechle et al. 1997, J Shoulder Elbow Surg 6(5):429-439: the posterior deltoid and infraspinatus had the largest horizontal extension moment arms), but no stable URL or PubMed id was found, so it is not cited and no row is added; the anatomy lane may add an assist row if it can cite it.

Second review: a teres minor selectivity claim could rest on Reinold et al. 2004 (PubMed 15296366: side-lying external rotation gave the most infraspinatus and teres minor activity of seven exercises), seen only as a search summary; not added.
section12Checks: Every node's §1.2 layer is supported; infraspinatus and teres minor outcrops are supported by Kenhub's relations text (see each node's layerCheck).

scapula.upward_rotation is a shoulders region action that no shoulders node performs; only the externals chest.serratus_anterior and back.upper_trapezius do (Physiopedia: the serratus anterior works with the upper and lower trapezius). Not a contradiction: §1.2 lists those externals for this reason.

shoulder.extension and shoulder.horizontal_adduction each have one own node (posterior deltoid prime; anterior deltoid assist); their main other movers are the externals (latissimus dorsi, teres major; pectoralis major).

databaseMuscle: the canonical name for the lateral deltoid is middle_deltoid (shared/capabilityRank.ts, server/fixtures/liveMuscleAggregation.ts), not lateral_deltoid. The groups have no canonical name.
Group layers: §1.2 gives '—'; AnatomicalLayer needs a value; suggested deltoid 'surface', rotator cuff 'deep'.

Role 'prime' is used where the references list the action as one of the part's own actions without 'helps' or 'assists'; it does not mean the main mover of that joint action across all muscles (for example, the anterior deltoid's internal rotation). The mappings lane should read it that way.

Second review: all eight region actions are already defined in shared/specialization/actions/joints.ts by wave 0; the dossier's actions[] now repeats the library's wording and the lane should not add actions/shoulders.ts for them.

Second review: every muscle node keeps a prime row, which regionContent.test.ts requires ('gives every muscle a main action'); demoting the supraspinatus's only row to assist, as Kenhub's 'assists the deltoid' would suggest, would fail that test.

Second review: shoulders.deltoid is kind 'muscle' with role 'group' (§1.2) and has no node actions, as a parent should not; but regionContent.test.ts 'gives every muscle a main action' filters on kind 'muscle' and role not 'adjacent', so as written it would fail on the deltoid (and on chest.pec_major, back.trapezius and upper_arm.triceps). The fix belongs in the test (skip role 'group', or any node that is a parent), not in the content; giving the deltoid prime rows would credit the parent beside its heads.
notes.aliasesNotAdded: 'medial deltoid' (used by Coratella 2020 and Campos 2020 for the lateral part) is said in a caveat rather than added as an alias, because 'medial' reads as the opposite direction.
notes.externals: chest.pec_major_clavicular, chest.pec_major_sternocostal, chest.serratus_anterior, back.upper_trapezius, back.latissimus_dorsi, back.teres_major were not researched; their home lanes own their claims.
notes.method: Web search only, on 19 Oct 2026; page fetches were not attempted beyond the known proxy refusal. 54 searches; every citation records the query and the excerpt relied on, copied from the search tool's generated summaries. An automated second review on 19 Oct 2026 ran 28 further searches with its own wording (secondReview.queries) and recorded each change it made (secondReview.changes).

secondReview.reviewer: Automated second review (an AI agent) with the same tools and limits as the first: web search only, page fetches refused, generated summaries that can misquote. Not peer review, and not a clinician or anatomist.
secondReview.scope: Every claim's sentences against its recorded excerpts; independent searches, in the reviewer's own words, for every selectivity and variation claim and for 7 of the 9 function claims (anterior, lateral and posterior deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis); source keys, URLs, titles, types and notes; node fields, node actions, roles, layers and outcrops against 10-multi-region.md §1.2.
secondReview.draftNote: No claim went to draft: every sentence the excerpts did not support was rewritten to what they support, and every disagreement found was stated in the wording with its source.
